blocks.text: Many circuits contain both capacitors and resistors. Fig 16.11 shows a resistor-capacitor (R-C) circuit. When the switch S is set to terminal A, the R-C combination is connected to a battery of voltage Vo, which charges the capacitor through the resistor R. The capacitor does not charge instantly; the charge builds up gradually to its equilibrium value qo = CVo. Fig 16.12 shows the growth of charge with time: q = 0 at t = 0 and rises gradually to qo. The voltage across the capacitor at any instant is V = q/C.

blocks.title: Time constant
blocks.text: How fast a capacitor charges or discharges depends on the product RC, which has the unit of time and is called the time constant. For charging, it is the time for the capacitor to reach 0.63 of its equilibrium charge qo. The smaller the time constant, the sooner the charge reaches its final value.

Fig 16.13 (a) shows discharging. With the switch at B, the charge +q on one plate flows round through the resistance and neutralises the charge -q on the other. The graphs of Fig 16.13 (b) show that discharging begins at t = 0 with q = CVo and the charge falls gradually to zero; a smaller time constant gives a faster discharge.

blocks.alt: Left: a circuit with a resistor R and a capacitor C in series, a two-way switch S with contacts A and B, and a battery Vo; with S at A the battery charges C through R, with S at B the capacitor discharges through R. Right top: charging graphs of q against t rising towards the dashed line qo = CVo, a red curve for small RC rising faster than a blue curve for large RC, with 0.63 qo reached at t = RC. Right bottom: discharging graphs falling from CVo, the small-RC curve falling faster.
blocks.caption: Charging and discharging a capacitor through a resistor (original diagram after Figs 16.11 to 16.13).
blocks.long_description: The resistor limits the current, so the capacitor charges and discharges gradually. The time constant RC sets the pace: after one time constant the charging capacitor has 63 per cent of its final charge.

blocks.text: The time constant of a series RC circuit is tau = RC. Show that an ohm times a farad is a second. Solution: by Ohm's law V = IR, and with I = q/t, V = (q/t) R, so R = Vt/q. Also C = q/V. Multiplying, RC = (Vt/q)(q/V) = t. So 1 ohm x 1 farad = 1 second.

blocks.prompt: A 1 kilo-ohm resistor and a 100 uF capacitor are in series. What is the time constant?

items: Charging through R: q rises gradually to qo = CVo.
Time constant RC (ohm x farad = second); 0.63 qo after RC.
Discharging: q falls from CVo; small RC means faster change.
